hero.title: Welcome to the CriptEnv Documentation

whatIs.title: What is CriptEnv?
whatIs.paragraph1: CriptEnv is an open-source secrets management platform with a Zero-Knowledge architecture. An alternative to Doppler and Infisical, it lets developers and teams manage environment variables, API keys and sensitive credentials with end-to-end encryption.
whatIs.paragraph2: All secrets are encrypted 100% client-side with AES-256-GCM. The server never receives plaintext data — even with full access to the database, it is impossible to decrypt your credentials.

zeroKnowledge.title: Zero-Knowledge
zeroKnowledge.description: Secrets are encrypted 100% client-side. The server stores only ciphertext — it never sees your real data.

consistent.title: Consistent
consistent.description: CLI and API share the same semantics. What you do in the terminal you can do over HTTP and vice versa.

secureByDefault.title: Secure by default
secureByDefault.description: AES-256-GCM with PBKDF2-HKDF. No plaintext in logs, no token exposure, no data compromise.

howItWorks.title: Zero-Knowledge — How does it work?

howItWorks.step4: The API receives only ciphertext, IV, auth tag, checksum and metadata.

inputs.title: Inputs
inputs.body: The Action accepts the following inputs:

inputs.vaultPassword: Project vault password (via GitHub Secrets). With it, the Action exports plaintext values; without it, variables receive the ciphertext.
inputs.environment: Target environment (e.g. production, staging). Default: production.
inputs.prefix: Prefix for the environment variables. Default: SECRET_.

overview.title: Security
overview.description: CriptEnv is built on a zero-knowledge architecture, so your environment secrets are never exposed to the server. All encryption happens on the client: the server only stores encrypted data that cannot be decrypted without the project's vault password.
overview.passwordCallout: The project vault password is never sent to the server. It is used locally to derive encryption keys that never leave your device.

confidentiality.title: Confidentiality
confidentiality.body: Every secret is encrypted with AES-256-GCM before it is stored or transmitted. The server never sees plaintext.

integrity.title: Integrity
integrity.body: AES-GCM provides built-in authentication (128-bit GCM auth tag), so any tampering with encrypted data is detected immediately on decryption.

isolation.title: Environment isolation
isolation.body: Each environment gets its own key, derived with HKDF from the vault key and the environment ID. A key from one environment cannot decrypt another environment's secrets.

bruteForce.title: Brute-force resistance
bruteForce.body: Key derivation uses PBKDF2 with 100,000 HMAC-SHA256 iterations, making brute-force attacks computationally expensive even with specialized hardware.

hierarchy.title: Key hierarchy
hierarchy.body: CriptEnv uses a well-defined key hierarchy to isolate environments and projects:

encryption.title: Encryption protocol
encryption.description: Technical details on algorithms, parameters and the full key-derivation flow.

zeroKnowledge.title: Zero-knowledge architecture
zeroKnowledge.description: How the zero-knowledge model protects your data, and what the server can and cannot see.

threatModel.title: Threat model
threatModel.description: Analysis of attack scenarios, risk levels and implemented mitigations.

zeroKnowledge.title: Zero-Knowledge Architecture
zeroKnowledge.description: CriptEnv's zero-knowledge architecture ensures the server never has access to your secret values in plaintext. All encryption and decryption happen exclusively on the user's client, using the project's vault password, which is never transmitted.
zeroKnowledge.simpleCallout: Put simply: even if the server were fully compromised, attackers would only get encrypted data, which is useless without the project's vault password.

what.title: What is zero knowledge?
what.p1: In CriptEnv, "zero knowledge" means the server can confirm you have the right password (through the vault proof) without ever learning that password or getting the keys derived from it.
what.p2: This differs from traditional systems where the server stores password hashes and the data: in CriptEnv, the encrypted values are useless even to whoever controls the server.

clientSide.title: How client-side encryption works
clientSide.body: The whole encryption process runs in the browser with the Web Crypto API:

visibility.title: What the server sees vs. doesn't see
visibility.sees:
✓ Ciphertext (values encrypted with AES-256-GCM)
✓ Variable names (keys) — only values are encrypted
✓ IVs (initialization vectors — not secret)
✓ Auth tags (GCM authentication tags)
✓ PBKDF2 salts (random per project, public by design)
✓ bcrypt hash of the vault proof
✓ Environment and project IDs (non-secret metadata)
✓ Creation and modification timestamps
✓ Organizational structure (projects, environments)
visibility.notSees:
✗ The project's vault password
✗ The derived vault key (PBKDF2 output)
✗ Environment keys (HKDF output)
✗ Environment variable values in plaintext
✗ Any ability to decrypt the values

proof.title: The vault proof mechanism
proof.body: The vault proof lets the server check that the user knows the right password without the password or the encryption keys ever being transmitted.
proof.callout: The proof is derived from the same vault password but with its own random salt (proof_salt), separate from the salt of the encryption key. So the proof cannot be used to derive the encryption key, and the server keeps only a bcrypt hash of it.

forgot.title: Forgot the password?
forgot.body: There is no recovery mechanism. Since the server never had your password or keys, the data cannot be recovered without them. This is a feature, not a bug: it ensures no one but you can read your secrets.

teams.title: Security for teams
teams.body: In shared setups, each member reaches only the projects they're authorized for, and decryption still happens on the client.

audit.title: Auditing
audit.body: The server can log access events (timestamps, IPs, environment IDs) without ever seeing the secret values. That enables security auditing without breaking the zero-knowledge architecture.

encryption.title: Encryption Protocol
encryption.description: CriptEnv uses a multi-layer key-derivation chain so that every environment has its own isolated encryption key. The whole process runs in the user's browser: the server never has the keys or the plaintext values.

flow.title: Key-derivation flow
flow.body: The full derivation follows these steps:

params.title: Cryptographic parameters

pbkdf2.title: PBKDF2 (vault key derivation)
pbkdf2.salt: 32 bytes (256 bits) — generated randomly per project when the vault is created

hkdf.title: HKDF (per-environment derivation)
hkdf.salt: Environment ID (UUID) — gives each environment a unique key

aes.title: AES-256-GCM (data encryption)
aes.algorithm: AES-256-GCM — authenticated encryption in Galois/Counter Mode
aes.keySize: 32 bytes (256 bits) — environment key derived with HKDF
aes.iv: 12 bytes (96 bits) — generated randomly for each encryption
aes.tag: 16 bytes (128 bits) — authentication tag for integrity checks

params.ivWarning: The IV (initialization vector) is generated randomly for every encryption. Never reuse an IV with the same key — that would break GCM's security.

proof.title: Vault proof derivation
proof.body: Besides the encryption key, CriptEnv derives a separate proof used to authorize vault writes in the API. It proves knowledge of the vault password without revealing the password or the encryption key.

storage.title: Local metadata vs. remote vault
storage.localBody: The CLI keeps local metadata in SQLite in the user's home directory:
storage.localCallout: The CLI's main flow does not store secrets locally. Secrets live in the remote vault and are decrypted only in memory.
storage.cloudBody: The cloud vault stores only already-encrypted values:

implementation.title: Implementation
implementation.body: Simplified example of the encryption flow with the Web Crypto API:

threatModel.title: Threat Model
threatModel.description: This page reviews the attack scenarios most relevant to CriptEnv, the risk level of each one and what the architecture does — and does not — protect against.
threatModel.assumption: The threat model assumes the attacker may fully control the server, database and infrastructure — but not the user's device.

database.title: Database compromise
database.impact: Ciphertext and variable names exposed; values unreadable without the vault password
database.scenario: Scenario: an attacker gets full access to the server database, including users, environments and stored secrets.

mitigations.0: Values stored only as AES-256-GCM ciphertext
mitigations.1: PBKDF2 salts and IVs are public by design
mitigations.2: Only a bcrypt hash of the vault proof is stored, never the password or keys
mitigations.3: Variable names (keys) are stored in plaintext — avoid putting secrets in names

database.result: Result: the stolen values are useless without the vault password. The remaining attack is an offline brute force on that password, slowed down by PBKDF2 — which is why a strong password matters.

admin.title: Malicious administrator
admin.impact: Can read metadata; could serve tampered web code to capture passwords
admin.scenario: Scenario: a server administrator or insider with privileged access tries to read user data.

mitigations.0: Stored values cannot be decrypted with what the server holds
mitigations.1: The CLI encrypts locally and does not run code served by the web app
mitigations.2: The code is open source, so the client logic can be reviewed

admin.result: Result: an administrator sees metadata (timestamps, IDs, variable names) but not the values. As in any web-based zero-knowledge app, whoever controls the server could ship altered JavaScript that captures the password typed in the browser; users who need to rule this out should use the CLI.

mitm.title: Man-in-the-middle (MITM)
mitm.impact: Traffic interception, but values travel already encrypted
mitm.scenario: Scenario: an attacker intercepts network traffic between the client and the server.

mitigations.1: HSTS to prevent downgrades to HTTP
mitigations.2: Values are encrypted before they are sent
mitigations.3: The vault password and derived keys never cross the network

mitm.result: Result: even with TLS broken, the attacker would only see AES-256-GCM ciphertext. A broken TLS could still expose session tokens, metadata and the web app's code.

xss.title: XSS (cross-site scripting)
xss.impact: Code running in the app could read data decrypted in memory
xss.scenario: Scenario: an attacker injects scripts that run in the context of the user's browser.

mitigations.1: React escapes rendered content by default

xss.result: Result: if an XSS succeeds despite these measures, the attacker could read secrets decrypted in memory and the vault password while it is typed during that session.

session.title: Session hijacking
session.impact: API access as the user, but only to encrypted data
session.scenario: Scenario: an attacker steals the user's session token and impersonates them on the server.

mitigations.1: Users can list and revoke their active sessions
mitigations.2: The vault password is not part of the session

session.result: Result: the attacker can call the API, but the data returned is encrypted. Without the vault password, nothing can be decrypted — though metadata could be read and data deleted until the session is revoked.

bruteForce.title: Brute force on the password
bruteForce.impact: Attempts to guess the vault password
bruteForce.scenario: Scenario: an attacker tries to guess the project's vault password by testing many combinations — online against the API, or offline with a stolen database.

mitigations.0: PBKDF2 with 100,000 iterations makes every attempt slow
mitigations.1: Random salt per project (prevents rainbow tables and attacking many vaults at once)
mitigations.2: Rate limiting on the API (online attempts only)
mitigations.3: AES-GCM auth tag makes a wrong password fail immediately

bruteForce.result: Result: at ~100 ms per attempt on one CPU core, testing 1 billion passwords takes about 3 years — and GPUs run many attempts in parallel. Rate limiting does not help against an offline attack, so security rests on a long, random password.

threatModel.userResponsibility: Your responsibility: the system's security fundamentally depends on the strength of the vault password. Use a long, unique password generated by a password manager. The zero-knowledge architecture cannot protect a weak or reused password.

overview.description: Manage your secrets straight from the terminal — with end-to-end encryption and zero knowledge on the server side.

terminal.title: Terminal-first
terminal.description: Every operation happens in your terminal. If you can open a shell, you can use CriptEnv.

zk.title: Zero-knowledge
zk.description: Your secret values are encrypted locally with AES-256-GCM before any sync. The server never sees them in plaintext.

remote.title: Remote vault
remote.description: The CLI works on the project's remote vault, keeping everything in sync with the web dashboard and the team.

secrets.title: Secret management
secrets.description: Store, rotate, import and export environment variables with strong encryption and versioning.

sync.title: Sync
sync.description: Push imports .env files into the remote vault; pull exports the remote vault to local files.

environments.title: Multiple environments
environments.description: Create and manage isolated environments (dev, staging, production) within one project.

cicd.title: CI/CD
cicd.description: Integrate with CI/CD pipelines. Log in headlessly, list secrets and deploy without exposing credentials.

integrations.title: Integrations
integrations.description: Connect cloud providers (Vercel, Render) and sync secrets automatically.

rotation.title: Rotation and expiration
rotation.description: Set expiration alerts and rotate keys with automatic versioning.

install.title: Quick install
install.requirements: Requires Python 3.10 or later. The CLI is cross-platform and runs on macOS, Linux and Windows.
install.after: After installing, see the <commands>Command Reference</commands> for every available option, or <configuration>Configuration</configuration> to understand the local layout.

commands.title: Command reference
commands.description: Full list of every command, option and usage example.

configuration.title: Configuration
configuration.description: Layout of ~/.criptenv/, the local session, the vault password and environment variables.

configuration.title: CLI configuration
configuration.description: Learn how the CriptEnv CLI works as a remote terminal, what data stays local and how to use environment variables in automation.

remote.title: Remote terminal
remote.body: The main commands work directly on the project's remote vault. The CLI downloads encrypted blobs, decrypts them in memory when needed, re-encrypts in its own process and sends only ciphertext to the API.
remote.callout: The backend never receives secret values in plaintext, and the project's vault password is never sent to the server.

local.title: Local layout
local.body: The ~/.criptenv/ directory holds only light metadata and local session credentials:
local.authKey: Local key used to protect CLI and CI session tokens.
local.vaultDb: SQLite database with the session, current project, metadata cache and compatibility tables.
local.backupWarning: The CLI's normal flow does not write a local copy of your secrets. Backups of ~/.criptenv/ still need protecting because they contain session credentials.

vaultPassword.title: Vault password
vaultPassword.body: The vault password belongs to the project. It derives the client-side encryption keys and is asked for only when a command needs to decrypt or change secrets.
vaultPassword.automation: For automation, set CRIPTENV_VAULT_PASSWORD. The CLI uses it instead of the interactive prompt.

envVars.title: Environment variables
envVars.project: Default project for commands that accept --project.
envVars.vaultPassword: Project vault password for non-interactive use.
envVars.apiKey: API key (cek_...) that authenticates the process directly, with no login and no session written to disk — suited to CI, containers and read-only HOME directories.
envVars.warning: Don't expose CRIPTENV_VAULT_PASSWORD in logs, shared shells or persistent histories. In CI, use the provider's secrets mechanism.

configuration.doctor: Use criptenv doctor to check the session, current project, local metadata and API connectivity.

commands.title: Command Reference
commands.description: Full documentation of every CriptEnv CLI command, organized by category.
commands.configurationLink: For more on configuring the CLI, see the <link>Configuration page</link>.

init.description: Prepares the ~/.criptenv/ directory and the local metadata database. Optional; it does not create a local secret vault or a master password.

login.description: Signs in to your CriptEnv account and stores the session token locally.

params.1: Email and password login, asking for the email interactively
params.3: Log in with an API key (cek_...). Also read from CRIPTENV_API_KEY; with no value, it prompts without echoing

logout.description: Ends the current session and removes the locally stored token.

doctor.description: Checks the local setup: database, permissions, connectivity and CLI version.

set.description: Encrypts a secret and stores it in the project's remote vault. Use the KEY=value syntax.

get.description: Decrypts a remote secret in memory and prints its value.

params.3: Copy the value to the clipboard

list.description: Lists every key in the remote vault without decrypting values.

delete.description: Permanently removes a secret from the remote vault.

params.0: Name of the secret to remove

rotate.description: Creates a new version of the secret. The previous version is kept for reference.

push.description: Imports a .env file into the remote vault. Without a file, the command fails and points you to import.

pull.description: Exports secrets from the remote vault to a local file. Without --output, the command fails and points you to export.

import.description: Imports secrets from a .env file into the remote vault.

export.description: Exports secrets from the remote vault to a .env or JSON file.

run.description: Runs a command with the environment's secrets injected as environment variables — without writing any file to disk. The child process's exit code is propagated.

diff.description: Compares a local .env file with the remote vault (drift detection) and exits with status 1 when they differ — useful as a CI gate. --show-values shows only a masked preview; full values are never printed.

envList.description: Lists every environment in the project.

projectsCreate.description: Creates a new project with a vault password.

ciSecrets.description: Lists the secrets available in the CI context.

ciDeploy.description: Imports a secrets file into the remote vault from a CI context.
ciDeploy.note: Requires CLI 0.2.2+, a CI token with the write:secrets scope and CRIPTENV_VAULT_PASSWORD: values are encrypted on the runner and the API only receives the blobs. Tokens restricted to one environment can only deploy to it.

params.2: Show what would be sent, without sending

ciTokensCreate.description: Creates a new CI/CD token. The token is shown only once.

params.2: Restrict the token to one environment

params.0: ID of the token to revoke

integrationsDisconnect.description: Disconnects an integration. Get the ID from integrations list.

params.0: ID of the integration to disconnect

integrationsSync.description: Syncs CriptEnv secrets with the connected provider.

secretsAlert.description: Sets up expiration alerts for a secret.

health.description: Public endpoints to check API availability. Useful for monitoring, load balancers and integration checks.
health.callout: These endpoints need no authentication and respond quickly, for infrastructure health checks.

status.title: API status
status.body: Returns the API's overall status. It always responds 200 while the server is up.

ready.title: Readiness
ready.body: Checks whether the API is ready to take requests, including database connectivity. Returns 200 when everything works, or 503 when the database is unreachable.

audit.description: Review the record of actions taken in the project. Audit logs track changes to the vault, secrets, environments, members, invitations, tokens, API keys and settings.
audit.callout: Reads (pull, get, export) are not logged; only changes are. Audit logs are removed together with the project or account.

list.title: List audit logs
list.body: Returns the project's audit logs, paginated and filterable. Each entry has the actor, action, affected resource, origin (auth_type) and timestamp.

params.action: Filter by action, e.g. vault.pushed, secret.rotated, member.added, member.role_changed, invite.created, token.created, api_key.created
params.resourceType: Filter by resource type, e.g. vault, environment, member, invite, integration, ci_token, api_key, project

invites.description: Manage email invitations to add new members to a project. Invitations expire after 7 days and are tied to a specific role.
invites.callout: Every endpoint below requires authentication and lives under /api/v1/projects/'{pid}'/invites. Creating and deleting invitations requires the admin role; the owner role cannot be granted through an invitation.

create.title: Create invitation
create.body: Emails an invitation to a new member (admin only). The invitation expires automatically after 7 days. The invite token is returned only in this response.

params.role: Member role: viewer, developer or admin

list.title: List invitations
list.body: Returns the project's invitations. Invitations revoked through the revoke endpoint are deleted permanently.

accept.title: Accept invitation
accept.body: Accepts a pending invitation. The authenticated user gets access to the project with the invitation's role.

revoke.title: Revoke invitation
revoke.body: Revokes a pending invitation and permanently removes the link. Developers can only revoke pending invitations they created; admins can revoke any.

delete.title: Delete invitation
delete.body: Permanently deletes an invitation from the project (admin only). Returns 204 with no body.

ciTokens.description: Authentication tokens for CI/CD pipelines. They start with ci_, can be limited to scopes and to one environment, and the plaintext value is shown only once, at creation. In the pipeline, the token is exchanged for a 1-hour session (ci_s_…).
ciTokens.vaultWarning: The token alone decrypts nothing: values are encrypted with the project's vault password. The pipeline needs the token and the vault password (for example, in the CRIPTENV_TOKEN and CRIPTENV_VAULT_PASSWORD secrets).

create.title: Create token
create.body: the token field only appears in this response.

params.name: Descriptive token name
params.environmentScope: Restricts the token to one environment (e.g. production), which must exist in the project. If omitted, it applies to all.

list.title: List tokens
list.body: Returns the project's tokens. The token value is never returned after creation.

revoke.title: Revoke token
revoke.body: Revokes the token immediately. Responds 204 No Content.

delete.title: Delete token
delete.body: Deletes the token permanently. Responds 204 No Content.

pipeline.title: Using the token in a pipeline
pipeline.body: Exchange the token for a 1-hour session and download the environment's encrypted blobs. Decryption happens on the client, with the vault password.
pipeline.callout: In practice, use the CLI (criptenv ci login) or the GitHub Action, which handle the exchange and decryption for you.

integrations.description: Connect CriptEnv to hosting providers to sync secrets. Available today: Vercel and Render (Railway coming soon).
integrations.callout: Sync works both ways: push sends CriptEnv secrets to the provider and pull imports them from the provider.

create.title: Create integration
create.body: Connects a new hosting provider integration. The provider token is stored encrypted on the server.

params.name: Integration name
params.config: Provider settings. Vercel: api_token and project_id. Render: api_token and service_id.

list.title: List integrations
list.body: Returns the project's integrations and the providers available to connect.

get.title: Get integration
get.body: Returns the details of one integration.

delete.title: Delete integration
delete.body: Removes the integration and its stored provider token. Returns 204 with no body.

sync.title: Sync
sync.body: Runs a sync between CriptEnv and the provider. Use push to send secrets to the provider or pull to import them.

params.secrets: Decrypted secrets to send to the provider. The server never decrypts the vault, so a push without this field sends nothing.

validate.title: Validate integration
validate.body: Checks that the connection to the provider works with the stored credentials.
